lesson_title: The impact of the First World War on Germany
content_html:
Germany Defeated: the World War One Legacy

When the guns fell silent on 11 November 1918, Germany did not surrender on the battlefield. German troops still occupied foreign soil, and many soldiers returned home undefeated. Yet within weeks, the Kaiser had abdicated, a republic had been proclaimed, and German politicians had signed an armistice. This disconnect between military reality and political outcome would poison German democracy for the next fifteen years.

Key Fact

The Treaty of Versailles (June 1919) imposed on Germany: war guilt (Article 231), reparations of £6.6 billion (set 1921), loss of 13% of territory, the Rhineland demilitarised, and the army limited to 100,000 men.

The Treaty of Versailles, 1919

The Treaty of Versailles was signed by the new German government on 28 June 1919. German representatives were not allowed to negotiate — they were simply handed the document and told to sign. The treaty's main terms were devastating:

War guilt: Article 231, the ‘War Guilt Clause’, forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for the war. This had enormous moral and financial consequences. Reparations: Germany was required to pay compensation for war damage. The final figure, set in 1921, was £6.6 billion — a sum many economists believed impossible to pay in full. Territorial losses: Germany lost 13% of its European territory, including Alsace-Lorraine (to France), Eupen and Malmedy (to Belgium), North Schleswig (to Denmark after a plebiscite), Posen and West Prussia (to the newly created Poland). Danzig became a free city under League of Nations supervision. German colonies were redistributed as ‘mandates’ among the Allies. Military restrictions: The German army was limited to 100,000 men, no tanks or aircraft, and the navy was stripped of its main fleet. The Rhineland was demilitarised.

Germans across the political spectrum condemned the treaty as a Diktat — a peace dictated by force rather than agreed by negotiation. Many had expected a settlement based on Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points, which promised national self-determination and no punitive terms. Instead they received humiliation. The army was outraged by the military clauses; industrialists feared reparations would cripple the economy; nationalists raged at territorial losses that left millions of German-speakers under foreign rule.

The politicians who signed the armistice in November 1918 were branded November Criminals by right-wing groups who claimed they had ‘stabbed Germany in the back’ by surrendering when the army could still have fought on. This ‘stab-in-the-back myth’ was historically false — the German High Command had itself requested an armistice because the military situation was hopeless — but it was politically powerful and would fuel right-wing resentment throughout the Weimar period.

The Birth of the Weimar Republic

On 9 November 1918, Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated and Friedrich Ebert of the Social Democrat Party (SPD) became head of government. Two days later, the armistice was signed. In February 1919, a new constitution was drawn up at Weimar, giving the republic its name. The Weimar Constitution created a democratic system with proportional representation, where seats in the Reichstag were allocated in direct proportion to votes cast. This ensured that even small parties gained representation, but it also meant coalition governments were the norm and decisive majorities were rare.

Key Fact

Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed the President to rule by emergency decree, bypassing the Reichstag. It was designed for genuine crises, but was used 136 times between 1930 and 1932, undermining parliamentary democracy.

Political Instability: the Spartacist Rising, 1919

The new republic faced violent opposition from both left and right from its first weeks. In January 1919, the Spartacists, led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, launched an armed uprising in Berlin. Inspired by the Bolshevik revolution in Russia, they seized newspaper offices and called on workers to overthrow the government. Ebert called in the Freikorps — right-wing volunteer ex-soldiers — to crush the revolt. The Freikorps suppressed the rising brutally; both Luxemburg and Liebknecht were murdered in custody in January 1919. The use of the Freikorps to defend the republic permanently alienated the German left from Ebert’s government.

Right-wing opposition erupted in March 1920 when the Kapp Putsch attempted to seize power in Berlin. Wolfgang Kapp, a nationalist politician, and General Walther von Lüttwitz marched Freikorps units into Berlin and declared a new government. The regular army refused to fire on the Freikorps. The Weimar government fled the capital. The putsch collapsed within four days when Berlin’s trade unions called a general strike that paralysed the city — transport, power and water all stopped. Kapp fled to Sweden. The episode revealed the fragility of the new republic: it had been saved not by its own security forces but by workers' industrial action.

The weakness of both putsches showed the deep divisions in German society. Left-wing workers, nationalist ex-soldiers, conservative businessmen and rural landowners had completely incompatible visions of Germany’s future. The Weimar Republic sat at the centre of these conflicts, lacking the broad popular legitimacy needed to command loyalty in a crisis.

Structural Weaknesses of the Weimar System

Beyond immediate crises, the republic had deeper structural problems. Proportional representation produced weak coalition governments that frequently collapsed. Between 1919 and 1933, Germany had twenty different cabinets. Article 48 gave the President emergency powers that could bypass parliament entirely. The judiciary and civil service were largely staffed by men loyal to the old imperial order, and treated the republic’s enemies with leniency: Hitler received a light sentence for his 1923 coup attempt, while left-wing defendants faced far harsher treatment. The army remained a ‘state within the state’, never fully committed to democratic government.

The Ruhr Crisis, 1923

By 1923, Germany had fallen behind on its reparations payments. In January 1923, French and Belgian troops marched into the Ruhr, Germany's industrial heartland, to seize coal and steel as payment in kind. The German government responded by ordering passive resistance — a general strike across the occupied zone. Workers stopped producing, officials refused to obey French orders, and sabotage became widespread. France responded with arrests, deportations and the shooting of protesters; thirteen workers died in the Krupp factory incident in Essen in March 1923.

Key Fact

The German government paid striking Ruhr workers by printing money. This decision, combined with a loss of industrial output, triggered hyperinflation: by November 1923, one US dollar was worth approximately 4.2 trillion German marks.

Hyperinflation, 1923

Hyperinflation had deep roots before 1923 — Germany had printed money to fund the First World War, and reparations demands had strained public finances since 1921 — but the passive resistance payments turned a serious inflation into a catastrophe. The government printed billions of marks to pay strikers who were producing nothing. Prices rose so fast that workers were paid twice daily and rushed to shops before prices increased again. Wheelbarrows of banknotes were required to buy bread. At the peak in November 1923, one US dollar was worth approximately 4.2 trillion marks.

The social effects were devastating but uneven. Those on fixed incomes — pensioners, civil servants, people with savings — saw their wealth wiped out. Debtors benefited: mortgage holders and factory owners who owed money could pay off their debts with near-worthless notes. Some wealthy businessmen actually gained from hyperinflation by buying up real assets cheaply. This redistribution of wealth created intense social resentment that would last for decades.

The crisis was resolved by Gustav Stresemann, who became Chancellor in August 1923. He called off passive resistance in September 1923, accepting the political cost of appearing to surrender to France, because he recognised the printing presses had to stop. In November 1923, a new currency — the Rentenmark — was introduced at a rate of one Rentenmark to one trillion old marks. The Rentenmark was backed by Germany’s land and industrial assets, giving it credibility where paper money had none. Hyperinflation ended almost immediately. The following year, Stresemann's government negotiated the Dawes Plan, which restructured reparations payments and unlocked US loans that began Germany's economic recovery.

The Munich Putsch, November 1923

The crisis of 1923 encouraged those who believed the Weimar Republic was finished. In Munich, Adolf Hitler — leader of the small Nazi Party — attempted to use the chaos to seize power. On the evening of 8 November 1923, he burst into a meeting at the Bürgerbräukeller, a large beer hall in Munich, fired a pistol into the ceiling, and declared a ‘national revolution’. He hoped to trigger a march on Berlin, modelled on Mussolini's March on Rome in 1922.

Key Fact

The Munich Putsch (8–9 November 1923) failed within 24 hours when police fired on the Nazi march at the Odeonsplatz. Sixteen Nazis and four police officers were killed. Hitler was arrested, tried, and sentenced to five years — but served only nine months, during which he dictated Mein Kampf.

The putsch failed for practical reasons: the Bavarian government and the army did not support it. Hitler had miscalculated the strength of loyalty to the republic among local authorities. However, the trial proved an unexpected propaganda gift. Hitler used the courtroom to attack the Weimar government as traitors and deliver nationalist speeches that were widely reported in the press. His light sentence — five years, of which he served nine months at Landsberg Prison — revealed the judiciary’s sympathy with right-wing nationalism.

While in prison, Hitler dictated Mein Kampf (‘My Struggle’), which outlined his ideology: extreme nationalism, anti-Semitism, the concept of Lebensraum, and the need for a dictatorial leader. He concluded that power could not be seized by force — it had to be won through the ballot box and legal means. This tactical shift would shape Nazi strategy throughout the late 1920s and early 1930s.

The year 1923 is often treated as a turning point in Weimar history precisely because multiple crises converged simultaneously. The Ruhr occupation, hyperinflation and the Munich Putsch all occurred within a single calendar year, and all three reflected the same underlying truth: Germany in 1923 was a republic in crisis, unloved by the left, hated by the right, and battered by forces largely beyond its control. That it survived — and even stabilised rapidly in 1924 with Stresemann’s currency reform and the Dawes Plan — is itself significant. The recovery that followed was real, but it rested on American loans and Stresemann’s personal diplomatic skill, both of which would disappear within six years. The psychological scars of 1923, particularly the middle class’s memory of their savings being wiped out, never fully healed and would resurface when economic crisis returned after 1929.

Gustav Stresemann and German Recovery

Gustav Stresemann dominated German foreign policy from 1923 until his death in October 1929. A former nationalist who had supported the war, he underwent a pragmatic conversion to the republic and concluded that Germany could only regain its place in the world through international co-operation rather than confrontation. His approach combined diplomatic skill with a willingness to make concessions, and it transformed Germany's international standing within six years.

Key Fact

The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured reparations into affordable annual payments and unlocked American loans totalling approximately 800 million gold marks. The Young Plan (1929) further reduced the total reparations bill and extended repayment to 1988.

Economic Recovery: the Dawes and Young Plans

In 1924, American banker Charles Dawes chaired a commission that proposed the Dawes Plan. Germany would receive large American loans, reparations payments were restructured into affordable annual instalments, and France agreed to withdraw from the Ruhr. The plan worked: US dollars flowed into Germany, industries modernised, unemployment fell, and real wages rose. By the mid-1920s, Germany was producing more steel than Britain. The Young Plan of 1929 went further: the total reparations bill was cut and repayment spread over nearly sixty years. These two agreements underpinned what appeared to be genuine economic stability.

However, this recovery rested on a fragile foundation — American short-term loans that could be recalled at any time. The Weimar economy was dangerously dependent on continued US investment. As Stresemann himself reportedly remarked privately, Germany was ‘dancing on a volcano.’ When Wall Street crashed in October 1929, American banks demanded their loans back, and the German economy collapsed almost immediately.

In 1925, Stresemann negotiated the Locarno Pact. Germany accepted its western borders (including the loss of Alsace-Lorraine to France) as permanent and agreed to resolve all disputes with its neighbours through arbitration rather than war. In return, France and Britain guaranteed the new borders and Germany was promised entry to the League of Nations. The ‘Spirit of Locarno’ marked Germany’s re-entry into the community of nations. French troops began withdrawing from the Rhineland ahead of schedule.

In 1926, Germany joined the League of Nations and was granted a permanent seat on its Council — the same status as Britain, France, Italy and Japan. This was a remarkable diplomatic achievement: Germany, defeated and humiliated in 1919, had become a respected member of the international order within seven years. Stresemann won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926.

Weimar Culture: a Creative Flourishing

The relative stability of the mid-1920s coincided with an extraordinary cultural flowering. Berlin became one of the most creative cities in the world. The Bauhaus school, founded by Walter Gropius in 1919, fused art, architecture and crafts into a revolutionary modernist aesthetic whose influence is still felt in design today. German cinema produced landmark works, including Fritz Lang’s Metropolis (1927) and F. W. Murnau’s Nosferatu (1922). Writers including Erich Maria Remarque (All Quiet on the Western Front, 1929) achieved international recognition.

Key Fact

Berlin's cabaret scene and nightlife became internationally famous, reflecting a new social freedoms in Weimar Germany. Women gained the vote in 1918, universities opened wider to women, and the 'New Woman' emerged as a cultural figure — though these changes were deeply controversial among conservative Germans.

Historians debate whether the Stresemann years deserve the label ‘golden age’. The recovery was real but uneven. Agricultural Germany struggled even in good times — falling grain prices hit farmers throughout the 1920s. Unemployment never fell below 1.3 million even in the best years. Political extremism did not disappear: the Nazis and communists remained active, and right-wing nationalists still regarded Versailles as an open wound. Coalition governments remained unstable. The cultural brilliance of Berlin coexisted with widespread poverty and social anxiety.

The period’s ‘golden’ quality depended almost entirely on American money and on Stresemann’s personal diplomatic skill. When Stresemann died in October 1929, just weeks before the Wall Street Crash, Germany lost both its economic lifeline and its most capable statesman simultaneously. The fragility of the recovery became apparent almost immediately.

Despite its achievements, the Stresemann era also contained the seeds of later crisis. The apparent stability masked deep political divisions: the Nazi Party, though marginal with only 2.6% of the vote in 1928, continued to operate; the Communist Party (KPD) was a significant force in industrial cities; and right-wing nationalist parties never accepted Locarno or the Dawes Plan as legitimate. The reparations question had not been resolved, only deferred. Germany’s continued resentment of Versailles meant that the international goodwill Stresemann had built could be reversed if the domestic political balance shifted. The mid-1920s stability was genuine, but it was also contingent on a set of international and economic conditions that proved temporary. When those conditions changed after 1929, the republic had no deep roots of popular loyalty to fall back on.

The Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression in Germany

On 24 October 1929, the New York Stock Exchange collapsed. American banks immediately recalled the short-term loans that had underpinned Germany’s recovery since 1924. German factories lost their credit, banks failed, and unemployment rocketed. By the winter of 1932, over six million Germans were officially unemployed — approximately one in three workers. Millions more were on short-time working. The social consequences were devastating: hunger, poverty, family breakdown, and a pervasive sense of hopelessness.

Key Fact

In the 1928 Reichstag election, the Nazi Party won just 2.6% of the vote. By July 1932, at the height of the Depression, they won 37.4% — becoming the largest party in the Reichstag, though still without a majority.

The Political Impact of the Depression

Chancellor Heinrich Brüning responded to the Depression with austerity: he cut wages, benefits and public spending, using Article 48 emergency decrees because he could not get his budget through the Reichstag. His measures deepened the depression rather than ending it. The human cost of austerity, combined with mass unemployment, turned millions of voters towards the political extremes. The Communist Party (KPD) grew significantly, but the Nazis grew far faster.

Hitler’s electoral appeal was remarkable in its breadth. He promised different things to different groups: jobs and economic recovery to the unemployed; protection of property and anti-communism to the middle classes and farmers; national greatness and revenge for Versailles to nationalists; strong leadership to those who saw coalition governments as weak and ineffectual. His speeches were emotionally charged, exploiting fear and resentment with extraordinary skill. The Nazi Party built a sophisticated propaganda machine, using modern techniques including radio, cinema and mass rallies.

The SA (Sturmabteilung), known as the Brownshirts, played a dual role. Their street violence — brawls with communists, attacks on Jewish businesses, disruption of opposition meetings — created an atmosphere of chaos. But paradoxically, this chaos helped the Nazis: voters who feared disorder were told that only Hitler could restore order. The SA also provided a sense of belonging and purpose to unemployed young men who had nothing else. By 1932, the SA had around 400,000 members.

Political violence escalated dramatically in 1932. In the summer of that year, there were hundreds of political killings on the streets of Germany. The Weimar Republic seemed unable to protect its citizens. This apparent weakness further discredited democratic government and pushed more voters towards parties that promised decisive action.

Elite Scheming: Papen, Hindenburg and Schleicher

By 1932, the Weimar political system was effectively deadlocked. The Nazis were the largest party but had no majority. The communists were strong. Moderate parties were weak. President Paul von Hindenburg, an elderly field marshal who privately despised Hitler, refused to appoint him Chancellor. Instead, he appointed Franz von Papen, a conservative aristocrat, in June 1932.

Key Fact

Franz von Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler as Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Papen believed he could control Hitler by surrounding him with conservative ministers. He was fatally wrong — within eighteen months Hitler had dismantled the entire constitutional order.

Historians have debated whether Hitler’s appointment was primarily the result of mass popular support or elite political miscalculation. Both factors mattered. The Nazis had the largest share of the popular vote (37.4% in July 1932, falling to 33.1% in November 1932 — a sign that support may have peaked). But Hitler became Chancellor not through a majority election victory but through the behind-the-scenes deal-making of Papen and Hindenburg. Papen calculated that he could use Hitler’s mass support while keeping real power in conservative hands. General Kurt von Schleicher, who briefly replaced Papen as Chancellor in December 1932, lost Hindenburg’s support and resigned in January 1933.

On 30 January 1933, Adolf Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany. The decision was made not by the German people through the ballot box but by an ageing president and a scheming ex-chancellor who fatally underestimated the man they thought they could control.

It is worth noting that Hitler never won a majority of the vote in a free election. The Nazis peaked at 37.4% in July 1932 and fell back to 33.1% in November 1932 as the worst of the Depression eased slightly and some voters returned to moderate parties. Had Hindenburg appointed a different Chancellor and stabilised the political situation, the Nazi surge might have continued to decline. The tragedy of January 1933 was that democracy was not overthrown from below by an unstoppable popular revolution — it was surrendered from above by conservative elites who calculated they had more to fear from communism than from Hitler, and who believed their money, institutions and social position would protect them once they had put him in office. They were catastrophically wrong on every count.

From Chancellor to Dictator

When Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, he did not yet have dictatorial power. Germany was still a constitutional republic. He had only two other Nazis in his twelve-man cabinet, and President Hindenburg retained the power to dismiss him. Within eighteen months, Hitler had eliminated all rivals, abolished all other political parties, and fused the offices of Chancellor and President. The speed and completeness of this transformation shocked even those who had expected him to be radical.

The Reichstag Fire and Emergency Decree, February 1933

On the night of 27 February 1933, the Reichstag building was set on fire. A young Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was found at the scene and arrested. Hitler immediately blamed the Communist Party for an organised plot to overthrow the state. Within hours, he had persuaded President Hindenburg to sign the Reichstag Fire Decree, which suspended freedom of speech, assembly, and the press, and allowed the police to arrest and detain anyone without trial. The communists were effectively outlawed. Over the following days, thousands of political opponents were arrested.

Key Fact

The Enabling Act (23 March 1933) passed by 444 votes to 94, with the SA lining the chamber. It gave Hitler the power to pass laws without the Reichstag's approval for four years — effectively making him a dictator within the bounds of the constitution.

The Enabling Act, March 1933

On 23 March 1933, the Reichstag voted on the Enabling Act. For it to pass, Hitler needed a two-thirds majority. He achieved this by having communist deputies arrested and by surrounding the Reichstag with SA stormtroopers to intimidate the remaining members. Only the Social Democrats voted against — their leader Otto Wels delivered a courageous speech defending democracy, knowing it would make no difference. The act passed by 444 votes to 94. Hitler now had the legal power to govern by decree.

Gleichschaltung (co-ordination) swept through German society over the following months. State governments were abolished and replaced by Nazi-appointed Reich governors. Trade unions were banned and replaced by the Nazi-controlled German Labour Front in May 1933. All political parties except the Nazis were dissolved or forced to disband by July 1933. Germany became a one-party state.

By 1934, the SA had grown to over two million members and its leader, Ernst Röhm, was demanding that the SA absorb the regular army and lead a ‘second revolution’ that would redistribute wealth. This alarmed conservative generals and industrialists whose support Hitler needed. On the night of 29–30 June 1934, the SS carried out mass arrests and executions across Germany. Röhm was murdered, as were many other SA leaders and political opponents, including former Chancellor Schleicher. Estimates of those killed range from several dozen to several hundred.

The Night of the Long Knives had two crucial effects. First, it destroyed the SA as an independent political force — it was subordinated to the SS and effectively domesticated. Second, it showed the German army that Hitler would protect their institutional interests, which secured military loyalty. The generals accepted what had happened because it served their own interests.

Key Fact

When President Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Hitler merged the offices of President and Chancellor, taking the title Führer (leader). The German army swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler as an individual — not to the German state or constitution — binding every soldier to him personally.

On 2 August 1934, President Hindenburg died. Within hours, Hitler announced that the offices of Chancellor and President had been merged into the new title of Führer. A plebiscite held on 19 August 1934 gave Hitler 89.9% of the vote in approval — though the conditions under which it was held made a free vote impossible. The personal oath of loyalty sworn by the army meant that any resistance to Hitler was now not merely illegal but a personal betrayal of a sacred vow. In just eighteen months, Hitler had dismantled the entire Weimar constitutional framework and concentrated all power in his own hands.

The speed of this consolidation is worth emphasising for exam purposes. Hitler exploited every crisis and opportunity methodically: the Reichstag Fire gave him a pretext to arrest communists before the March elections; the Enabling Act gave him legal cover for dictatorship; Gleichschaltung dismantled every independent institution before opposition could organise; and the Night of the Long Knives eliminated internal rivals while securing the loyalty of the one institution — the army — that could theoretically have stopped him. Each step was legally dressed in constitutional language even as it destroyed constitutional norms. This use of ‘legal revolution’ was precisely what Hitler had drawn from the failure of the Munich Putsch in 1923: raw force alone was insufficient; he needed the appearance of legitimacy to neutralise conservative resistance until it was too late to matter.

Nazi Economic Policy: Reducing Unemployment

When Hitler came to power in January 1933, approximately six million Germans were unemployed. Reducing unemployment was the Nazis' most visible domestic success and a crucial source of their popularity. They achieved it through a combination of public works, rearmament, and labour service schemes. By 1938, official unemployment had fallen to below one million, though the actual figure was higher because women and Jewish workers had been excluded from the count.

Key Fact

The Nazis reduced unemployment through the RAD (Reichsarbeitsdienst — National Labour Service, 1935), which required young men to complete six months of labour service; a massive autobahn road-building programme; and rapid rearmament from 1935.

Public Works and the Autobahns

The autobahns became the most visible symbol of Nazi economic achievement. Construction began in 1933 and provided employment for hundreds of thousands of workers. The project was heavily promoted as evidence of National Socialist modernity and organisational power. In practice, the number employed directly on autobahn construction was smaller than propaganda claimed, and rearmament did far more to reduce unemployment; but the motorways became a powerful image of national renewal.

The RAD (Reichsarbeitsdienst) required all young men aged 18 to 25 to complete six months of compulsory labour, typically on agricultural or construction projects. Workers received food, accommodation and a small wage, but primarily the programme was about discipline, ideological training and removing young men from the unemployment statistics.

Strength Through Joy (Kraft durch Freude, KdF) provided workers with leisure activities — subsidised holidays, theatre tickets, concerts, and cruises — as a substitute for the trade union rights that had been abolished in May 1933. Workers could save towards a Volkswagen car (though none were delivered before the war). These benefits were real: millions of Germans experienced holidays they could never have afforded before. The Beauty of Labour scheme improved workplace conditions, adding canteens, showers, and sports facilities to factories. Both programmes worked to win worker loyalty without giving workers any genuine economic power.

Women in Nazi Germany: the Three Ks

Nazi ideology prescribed a specific role for women, captured in the phrase Kinder, Küche, Kirche (children, kitchen, church). Women were to be wives and mothers first; their role was to produce children for the German nation. Women were pushed out of professional jobs, discouraged from higher education, and rewarded with the Mother’s Cross for having large families (bronze for four children, silver for six, gold for eight or more). The marriage loan scheme (introduced 1933) gave newly-wed couples a loan of 1,000 Reichsmarks, with a quarter of it cancelled for each child born.

In practice, Nazi policy towards women was contradictory. The economy increasingly needed female labour as rearmament expanded. By the late 1930s, the regime was quietly encouraging women back into the workforce — especially in nursing, farming and munitions factories — while still officially promoting the domestic ideal. Women’s experiences of the Nazi period varied enormously depending on class, region and individual circumstance.

Key Fact

The Hitler Youth (Hitlerjugend) for boys aged 14–18 and the League of German Girls (BDM, Bund Deutscher Mädel) for girls aged 14–18 became compulsory from March 1939. Younger children went to the German Young People (Deutsches Jungvolk) and Jungmädel respectively.

Schools were used to indoctrinate the next generation. All teachers had to join the Nazi Teachers’ League and follow revised curricula. History lessons emphasised Germany’s past greatness, Versailles as a crime, and the Nazi rise as a national salvation. Biology introduced racial theory, presenting the Jews as a biologically inferior race. Physical education received far more timetable time. Girls’ education emphasised domestic science and preparation for motherhood.

The Hitler Youth supplemented school with outdoor activities, sport, military drill and ideological instruction. It offered genuine fun — camping, hiking, competitions — alongside the propaganda. Membership grew from around 100,000 in 1933 to over seven million by 1939. For many boys, it provided a strong sense of belonging and purpose. However, by the late 1930s, compulsory membership had eroded enthusiasm and some young people expressed subtle resistance through ‘Swing Youth’ groups that preferred American jazz and British swing music to Nazi ideology.

lesson_title: Racial policy: Nazi treatment of the Jews to 1939
content_html:
Nazi Racial Ideology and the Jews

At the heart of Nazi ideology was a virulent anti-Semitism. Hitler had argued in Mein Kampf that Jewish people were a separate and inferior race responsible for Germany’s defeat in 1918 and for the evils of communism and international capitalism. This was not merely personal hatred — it was a systematic ideology that divided humanity into a racial hierarchy with ‘Aryan’ Germans at the top and Jewish people at the bottom. This ideology shaped Nazi policy from the moment Hitler took power.

Before 1933, there were approximately 523,000 Jews in Germany, making up less than one percent of the population. They were a largely assimilated community — many were professionals, academics, lawyers, doctors and businesspeople who considered themselves German first. The persecution they faced after 1933 came not from popular demand, but was driven from above by the state, though it built on existing social prejudices that the Nazis deliberately inflamed.

Key Fact

The Nuremberg Laws (September 1935) stripped Jews of German citizenship and banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jews. They legally defined who was Jewish based on grandparentage, creating a bureaucratic framework for racial persecution.

Early Persecution: the 1933 Boycott

On 1 April 1933, the Nazi regime organised a national boycott of Jewish-owned businesses. SA stormtroopers stood outside Jewish shops, law offices and medical practices, intimidating customers and painting ‘Jude’ (Jew) on windows. The boycott lasted only one day because of international criticism and because many Germans did not observe it; but it signalled the regime’s intentions. Over the following months, Jews were expelled from the civil service under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service (April 1933), removed from journalism, broadcasting and the arts, and excluded from many professions.

At the Nazi Party rally in Nuremberg in September 1935, Hitler announced two new laws that fundamentally altered the legal status of Jewish people in Germany. The Reich Citizenship Law stripped Jews of German citizenship, making them ‘subjects of the state’ rather than full citizens. The Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jews. Together, the Nuremberg Laws provided a legal framework for racial separation. Supplementary decrees defined who was ‘Jewish’ on the basis of grandparentage, creating categories of full Jews, half-Jews and quarter-Jews with different legal statuses.

Aryanisation and Economic Exclusion

Aryanisation was the forced transfer of Jewish-owned businesses into non-Jewish hands. Initially informal pressure and intimidation persuaded many Jewish business owners to sell cheaply; from 1937, the process became more systematic and legally enforced. Jewish professionals were progressively barred from their occupations. Jewish children were expelled from German schools. By late 1938, Jews had been almost entirely excluded from German economic life.

Key Fact

Kristallnacht (the Night of Broken Glass), 9–10 November 1938: approximately 7,500 Jewish businesses were smashed, around 400 synagogues were burned, at least 91 Jews were killed, and approximately 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps. The name refers to the broken glass that covered the streets.

On 7 November 1938, a young Jewish man, Herschel Grynszpan, shot a German diplomat in Paris, Ernst vom Rath, in protest at the deportation of his parents from Germany. When vom Rath died on 9 November, Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels used it as a pretext to orchestrate nationwide violence. SA and SS units, directed by the Nazi Party, attacked Jewish property across Germany. The violence was presented as a spontaneous popular reaction.

The aftermath was as devastating as the night itself. Jews were collectively fined one billion Reichsmarks for the damage done to their own property. Jewish emigration was officially encouraged — Jews were pressured to leave Germany but could only take a fraction of their assets. By September 1939, approximately half of Germany’s pre-1933 Jewish population had emigrated. The violence of Kristallnacht shocked international observers, though it produced no effective international response.

Historians describe the period 1933 to 1939 as one of escalating but not yet fully systematic persecution. The pattern was one of incremental radicalisation: each measure normalised the next. The 1933 boycott introduced public identification of Jews as targets; professional exclusions separated them from mainstream economic life; the Nuremberg Laws gave racial separation a legal framework; Aryanisation destroyed their economic independence; and Kristallnacht demonstrated that the state would use open violence with impunity. The international community’s muted reaction to Kristallnacht — expressions of horror but no sanctions, no military threat — was a signal that the regime noted. After September 1939, under the cover of war, persecution would escalate still further into systematic mass murder. Understanding the pre-war period is essential to understanding how that escalation became possible.

lesson_title: Terror and persuasion: how the Nazis controlled Germany
content_html:
Two Pillars of Nazi Control

Historians of Nazi Germany distinguish between two systems of control that reinforced each other: terror (the threat and use of violence) and persuasion (propaganda, education and cultural control). Neither alone would have been sufficient — a regime relying purely on terror exhausts itself and breeds resentment, while a regime relying purely on persuasion cannot suppress determined opposition. The Nazis combined both with remarkable effectiveness throughout the 1930s.

The SS and Heinrich Himmler

The SS (Schutzstaffel) began as Hitler’s personal bodyguard but grew under Heinrich Himmler into a vast security empire. By the late 1930s, Himmler controlled the SS, the Gestapo, the concentration camp system, and ultimately most of Germany’s police forces. SS membership was based on racial purity requirements as well as loyalty — members had to prove Aryan ancestry. The SS presented itself as an elite within an elite, a new racial aristocracy.

Key Fact

The Gestapo (Geheime Staatspolizei — secret state police) had around 32,000 officers in 1939 for a population of approximately 80 million. It operated largely on the basis of denunciations — ordinary Germans informing on neighbours, colleagues and family members — rather than a vast network of spies.

The Gestapo could arrest, imprison and send people to concentration camps without trial or appeal. It was particularly feared because of the power of self-censorship it induced: people never knew who might report them, so many refrained from expressing any dissent even privately. Modern historical research has emphasised that the Gestapo was actually relatively small — most of its intelligence came from citizens voluntarily denouncing others. Some denouncers were motivated by genuine ideological commitment; many others had personal grievances they used the Gestapo to settle.

The legal system was restructured to serve the regime. The People’s Court (Volksgerichtshof), established in 1934, handled political cases with hand-picked Nazi judges. Its notorious president, Roland Freisler, conducted show trials characterised by theatrical denunciations of defendants. Appeal to any ordinary court was impossible. Ordinary courts also reflected Nazi ideology — judges who showed leniency to political offenders were replaced.

Goebbels and the Propaganda Ministry

Joseph Goebbels was appointed Minister for Public Enlightenment and Propaganda in March 1933. He immediately established control over all means of mass communication. All journalists, writers, artists, musicians and filmmakers were required to join the Reich Chamber of Culture — those excluded (mainly Jews and political opponents) could not work. Goebbels understood that the most effective propaganda did not feel like propaganda: it entertained as well as indoctrinated.

Key Fact

The Nazis promoted the Volksempfänger ('People's Receiver') — a cheap radio set — so that by 1939 approximately 70% of German households owned one. Radio broadcasts were controlled by the state, giving Goebbels direct access to German living rooms. Cinema newsreels preceded every film, and the Propaganda Ministry approved all film productions.

The annual Nuremberg rallies were the most spectacular public events of the Nazi era. Hundreds of thousands attended; searchlights created a ‘cathedral of light’ effect; massed formations of Hitler Youth and SA presented an image of total national unity. Leni Riefenstahl’s 1935 film Triumph of the Will documented the 1934 rally and became one of the most influential propaganda films ever made. The rallies communicated the message that resistance was futile against such overwhelming force.

Censorship was total. Newspapers were required to follow a daily list of approved stories from the Propaganda Ministry. Books considered dangerous were burned in public ceremonies in May 1933 — works by Jewish authors, Marxists, pacifists and others were destroyed. Modern art (labelled degenerate art) was removed from galleries and displayed in a deliberately mocking exhibition in 1937. Only art celebrating Nazi themes, German landscapes, heroic workers and racial purity was permitted.

The interaction between terror and propaganda was more subtle than it might appear. Propaganda was most effective not where people were forced to believe it but where it reinforced things Germans already wanted to believe: that the Depression was ending, that national humiliation was being reversed, that a strong leader was restoring order. Economic recovery after 1933 gave propaganda real material to work with. The Gestapo’s power, meanwhile, rested less on its actual size — approximately 32,000 agents for 80 million people was far smaller than many assumed — than on the fear of denunciation by neighbours. This fear was the regime’s most cost-effective tool. Most Germans were not watched; they policed themselves, avoiding political conversations, keeping dissenting thoughts private, performing compliance whether they felt it or not. This combination of genuine support among many, passive compliance among most, and terror-induced silence among the rest proved remarkably stable throughout the 1930s.

lesson_title: Hitler's foreign policy and the road to war
content_html:
Hitler's Foreign Policy Aims

Hitler’s foreign policy goals were clearly stated in Mein Kampf (1925) and never fundamentally changed. He wanted to: destroy the Treaty of Versailles and restore German greatness; unite all German-speaking peoples in a greater German state; and conquer Lebensraum (living space) in eastern Europe by defeating the Soviet Union and enslaving or expelling its Slavic population. The foreign policy of 1933 to 1939 represented a step-by-step movement towards these goals, exploiting the weakness and reluctance of Britain and France to risk another war.

Key Fact

Key dates: rearmament publicly announced 1935; conscription reintroduced 1935; Rhineland reoccupied March 1936; Anschluss (union with Austria) March 1938; Sudetenland ceded (Munich Agreement) September 1938; Nazi-Soviet Pact signed August 1939.

Rearmament and Conscription, 1935

From the moment he came to power, Hitler began secretly rearming Germany in violation of the Treaty of Versailles. In March 1935, he publicly announced German rearmament and the reintroduction of conscription. He now planned to build an army of 550,000 men — far above the 100,000 limit set by Versailles. Britain, France and Italy condemned this at the Stresa Conference, but took no action. Britain actually signed the Anglo-German Naval Agreement in June 1935, limiting Germany’s fleet to 35% of Britain’s but in effect accepting German rearmament. Hitler correctly concluded that the Western powers would not stop him by force.

In March 1936, Hitler ordered German troops to march into the Rhineland, which had been demilitarised under Versailles and the Locarno Pact. This was Hitler’s biggest gamble up to that point: his generals were deeply nervous, and the troops had orders to withdraw if France resisted. France and Britain protested but did not act militarily. Hitler later said that the 48 hours after the march were the most nerve-wracking of his life, and that a French advance would have forced a German retreat.

The lack of Allied response enormously boosted Hitler’s confidence and domestic prestige. The German public was jubilant: troops had marched into German territory without a single shot being fired. The Rhineland success confirmed Hitler’s belief that the Western powers could be faced down. It also secured Germany’s western frontier and freed him to plan expansion eastward.

The Anschluss, March 1938

In March 1938, Hitler achieved the union of Germany and Austria. The Anschluss had been banned by the Treaty of Versailles, but Hitler exploited the Nazi movement within Austria, pressured Austrian Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg into resignation, and sent German troops across the border on 12 March 1938. Schuschnigg had attempted to hold a plebiscite on Austrian independence, but Hitler forced him to cancel it. German troops were greeted with genuine enthusiasm by many Austrians. A subsequent plebiscite reportedly showed 99% support for union — though conducted under Nazi conditions that made a free vote impossible. Britain and France issued protests but did not act.

Key Fact

At the Munich Conference (29–30 September 1938), Britain, France and Italy agreed to give Hitler the Sudetenland — the German-speaking border region of Czechoslovakia — without consulting the Czech government. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain returned claiming to have secured 'peace for our time'.

The Sudetenland crisis of summer 1938 arose from Hitler’s demands that the three million German-speakers in western Czechoslovakia be incorporated into Germany. Britain and France, desperate to avoid war, agreed at Munich to hand the region over without Czech participation. Hitler had promised this would be his last territorial demand. Within six months, in March 1939, he broke this promise and invaded the rest of Czechoslovakia — the first acquisition of non-German-speaking territory and the moment that convinced Britain and France that appeasement had failed.

In August 1939, Hitler neutralised the Soviet threat to his eastern flank by signing the Nazi-Soviet Pact with Stalin on 23 August 1939. The pact shocked the world — ideological enemies had made a deal. A secret protocol divided eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of influence. Hitler now had a free hand in the west. On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Two days later, Britain and France declared war on Germany.

A key theme in evaluating Hitler’s foreign policy is the relationship between his long-term goals and the opportunities created by Western appeasement. Historians debate whether Hitler followed a fixed programme laid out in Mein Kampf, moving methodically from Versailles revision to Lebensraum, or whether he was an opportunist who improvised within a broad ideological framework. What is clear is that the Western powers’ consistent reluctance to use force — driven by memories of the catastrophic losses of 1914–1918 and the genuine belief that some German grievances over Versailles were legitimate — gave Hitler the room to escalate with each unchallenged success. The Rhineland, Anschluss and Sudetenland all followed the same pattern: a demand, a crisis, a concession, and Hitler’s confidence growing with every capitulation. It was only when he invaded the non-German-speaking rump of Czechoslovakia in March 1939 that this pattern broke and Britain and France concluded that no further concessions were possible.

Why Do Historians Interpret Nazi Germany Differently?

Historians of Nazi Germany disagree not only about what happened, but about how to explain it — who was responsible, whether events were planned or improvised, and how ordinary Germans related to the regime. These disagreements arise from several sources: new evidence becoming available over time (especially after the opening of East German and Soviet archives after 1989); changing moral and political contexts in which historians write; different methods and theoretical frameworks; and genuine uncertainty in the surviving sources themselves.

For your examination, the most important debates concern: the intentionalist versus functionalist argument about Hitler’s role; the work of named historians including Alan Bullock, Ian Kershaw and Daniel Goldhagen; and the question of how much ordinary Germans knew about and supported the regime’s most extreme actions.

Key Fact

Intentionalists argue that Nazi policy — including the racial persecution of Jews — was planned from the beginning and driven by Hitler's own fixed ideology as laid out in Mein Kampf. Functionalists argue that policy evolved through improvisation, bureaucratic competition and chaotic decision-making rather than a master plan.

The Intentionalist Interpretation

The intentionalist interpretation places Hitler at the centre of everything. Historians such as Lucy Dawidowicz argued that Hitler had a clear programme — a consistent ideological plan — that he pursued systematically from his earliest writings. On this view, the persecution of Jews escalated from boycotts (1933) to the Nuremberg Laws (1935) to Kristallnacht (1938) because Hitler intended from the beginning to destroy the Jewish people of Europe. Intentionalists point to Mein Kampf as evidence that Hitler’s goals were clear and consistent throughout.

The functionalist (or structuralist) interpretation, developed by historians such as Martin Broszat and Hans Mommsen, emphasises the chaotic structure of the Nazi state. Rather than a well-organised machine implementing a master plan, they saw a system of competing agencies — the SS, the SA, various party offices, state ministries — all pursuing their own interests and jostling for Hitler’s favour. Policy evolved not from above but from below, through this competition, and Hitler’s role was often to ratify decisions others had already taken rather than to plan them in advance.

Functionalists argue that Mein Kampf should be read as political propaganda rather than a master blueprint. Hitler’s personal role in day-to-day decision-making was often less decisive than intentionalists claim. The extreme direction of policy — such as the eventual decision about Jews during the war — was the result of accumulated pressure from competing agencies and the radicalising dynamics of war, not a plan Hitler had held for decades.

Key Historians: Bullock, Kershaw, Goldhagen

Alan Bullock, in his influential 1952 biography Hitler: A Study in Tyranny, portrayed Hitler as a calculating opportunist — someone who used ideology cynically when useful but who was driven primarily by a hunger for power. Bullock emphasised Hitler’s tactical skill and personal agency. In his later work, Bullock compared Hitler and Stalin as parallel totalitarian leaders.

Key Fact

Ian Kershaw introduced the concept of 'working towards the Führer' — officials and ordinary Germans anticipating Hitler's wishes and acting on them without direct orders. Daniel Goldhagen's Hitler's Willing Executioners (1996) controversially argued that ordinary Germans participated in the Holocaust because of deeply held 'eliminationist anti-Semitism'.

Ian Kershaw’s two-volume biography of Hitler (1998 and 2000) is widely regarded as the definitive modern account. Kershaw synthesised intentionalist and functionalist insights, arguing that Hitler’s ideology was real and consistent, but that policy radicalised through a process of officials ‘working towards the Führer’ — anticipating what he wanted and competing to please him — rather than receiving step-by-step instructions. This concept explains how extreme policies could develop without a formal master plan.

Daniel Goldhagen’s Hitler’s Willing Executioners (1996) was controversial from its publication. Goldhagen argued that the perpetrators of mass violence against Jews were not coerced or blindly obedient, but were willing participants motivated by what he called ‘eliminationist anti-Semitism’ — a specifically German cultural attitude that viewed Jews as a mortal threat requiring extermination. Critics argued that Goldhagen overstated the uniqueness of German anti-Semitism and ignored evidence of perpetrators from other nations. The debate about ordinary German participation remains one of the most contested in the field.

Pulling It All Together: Germany 1919–1939

This lesson is about using everything you have learned about Germany in transition to answer the exam questions confidently. The exam tests three main skills: knowledge and understanding (recall and understanding), historical analysis (explanation and analysis), and source and interpretations work (source analysis/interpretation analysis). Most students lose marks not because they lack knowledge but because they apply the wrong skill to the wrong question type.

Source Utility (5 marks): the Three-Strand Method

A source utility question asks how useful a source is for a specific enquiry. The most common mistake is to judge a source purely by whether its author was biased. Examiners want three strands of evaluation:

1. Content: What does the source actually say or show that is relevant to the enquiry? Refer to specific details from the source. 2. Provenance: Who created the source, when, why, and for what audience? Does this make the source more or less useful — not just ‘biased’, but specifically how does the provenance affect what the source tells us? 3. Your own contextual knowledge: What do you know about the topic that helps you judge whether the source’s content is accurate, typical or unusual? This is the strand most students omit.

Key Fact

Top-band source utility answers integrate all three strands — content, provenance and contextual knowledge — into a single judgement about how useful the source is for a specific enquiry. A source can be very useful despite being biased if its bias tells us something important about the time.

Imagine a question: ‘How useful is a 1936 Nazi propaganda poster showing a heroic German worker alongside the slogan “Work and Bread” for understanding what the Nazis wanted Germans to believe about their economic policy?’ A top-band answer might work like this:

Content: The poster tells us the Nazis associated their regime with solving unemployment. The image of the heroic worker suggests pride in labour; the ‘Work and Bread’ slogan links the regime directly to economic recovery. This is directly relevant to the enquiry about what the Nazis wanted people to believe. Provenance: As a propaganda poster produced by Goebbels’ ministry in 1936, when unemployment had already fallen significantly from its 1932 peak, this is very useful for the enquiry — it shows precisely the message the Nazis wanted to project. The fact it is propaganda means it won’t show us the full picture (women excluded from unemployment figures, Jewish workers lost their jobs), but that is exactly what the enquiry asks us to judge. Context: We know that unemployment did fall from six million (1933) to under one million (1938), so the poster’s message was grounded in real economic change — though that change relied on rearmament and had significant social costs.

Compare Interpretations (10 marks): Focus on WHY

The Compare Interpretations question is the one most students answer badly. They describe what each interpretation says and then say the authors ‘had different opinions’. Examiners want to know WHY: what about the authors’ different purposes, methods, sources, time of writing, or national contexts explains why they emphasise different things?

For Germany 1919–1939, interpretations often differ on: Hitler’s personal role (intentionalism vs functionalism); how ordinary Germans related to the regime; whether economic recovery was genuine or illusory; the degree of terror versus consent in maintaining control. When practising, ask for each interpretation: when was it written? (availability of sources), who wrote it? (their standpoint, training, nationality), and what evidence did they emphasise?

Key Fact

In the Compare Interpretations question, you must explain WHY interpretations differ — the causes of the difference (author, purpose, sources, time of writing) — not just HOW they differ (what each says). Explaining only 'how' caps you below the top band.

For the 12-mark ‘Evaluate an Interpretation’ question, you must use your own contextual knowledge to both agree and disagree with the given interpretation before reaching a substantiated judgement. Pure agreement or pure disagreement caps your mark. For the 16-mark essay, top-band answers require a sustained judgement weighing different factors — not just covering both sides but reaching a reasoned conclusion about which factor or factors were most important and why.

A useful planning frame: PEEL each paragraph — Point (your claim), Evidence (specific detail from Germany 1919–1939), Explain (how the evidence supports the point), Link (relate back to the question or weigh against the counter-argument). In the conclusion, go beyond ‘both sides have valid arguments’ — state which side is stronger and why, with a piece of evidence that clinches the argument.

content_html:
The Open Door: Immigration Before 1920

In the decades before the First World War, the United States operated what was often called an open door policy on immigration. Between 1880 and 1914, approximately 20 million people arrived in the United States, many of them coming through Ellis Island in New York harbour. The majority came from southern and eastern Europe — Italians, Poles, Russians and Jews fleeing poverty or persecution. Many settled in crowded urban neighbourhoods, taking low-paid factory work. By 1910, over a third of the United States’ population was either foreign-born or the children of immigrants.

Not everyone welcomed this wave of newcomers. Many native-born Americans feared economic competition for jobs and wages. Some held deeply racist beliefs, arguing that immigrants from southern and eastern Europe were racially inferior to those from northern and western Europe. These views fed a growing demand for restrictions on immigration.

Key Fact

Between 1880 and 1914, roughly 20 million immigrants entered the United States. The majority came from southern and eastern Europe, and many passed through Ellis Island. This huge influx fuelled a nativist backlash that eventually produced major immigration restrictions in the 1920s.

Restricting Immigration: The Acts of 1921 and 1924

Congress responded to anti-immigration pressure with two landmark laws. The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 introduced national origin quotas for the first time, capping each nationality’s annual intake at 3 per cent of that nationality’s population already in America as recorded in the 1910 census. This reduced total immigration to around 357,000 per year — a sharp drop from the pre-war peak of over a million annually.

Three years later, the Immigration Act of 1924 tightened restrictions further. It cut the quota to 2 per cent of each nationality’s 1890 census figure — a deliberate choice, because far fewer southern and eastern Europeans lived in America in 1890. The act also set an annual cap of 164,667 immigrants and imposed a near-total ban on Asian immigration. The practical effect was to favour immigration from Britain, Germany and Scandinavia while drastically limiting arrivals from Italy, Poland and Russia.

Behind the quota system lay nativism — a fear that immigrants were changing the character of the United States. Influential works such as Madison Grant’s The Passing of the Great Race (1916) argued, using pseudo-scientific racial theory, that immigration from southern and eastern Europe would lead to racial and cultural decline. Such ideas had a real influence on legislators and public opinion during the 1920s.

Economic anxieties also played a role. After the First World War, many returning soldiers found that immigrants had taken their factory jobs. Trade unions, particularly the American Federation of Labor, lobbied for restrictions to protect wage levels. The combination of racial prejudice and economic competition made immigration restriction broadly popular across American society.

The Red Scare, 1919–1920

The end of the First World War brought a new fear to the United States: communism. The Bolshevik Revolution in Russia in 1917 had brought a communist government to power, and in 1919, a wave of strikes and bomb attacks across American cities stoked alarm that a similar revolution was being plotted at home. This period of panic became known as the First Red Scare.

In April 1919, postal workers intercepted packages containing letter bombs addressed to prominent politicians and businessmen. In June, simultaneous bombings in eight cities targeted government officials. Although the perpetrators were never fully identified, the attacks were widely blamed on anarchist and communist immigrants. Fear of foreign-born radicals merged with the existing anti-immigration mood.

Key Fact

The Palmer Raids of November 1919 and January 1920, led by Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, resulted in the arrest of approximately 10,000 suspected radicals across 33 cities. Hundreds were deported without trial. The raids alarmed civil liberties groups and were later criticised as unlawful.

The Palmer Raids

Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer responded to the bombing campaign by launching a series of raids on suspected radical organisations. The Palmer Raids took place in November 1919 and on the night of 2–3 January 1920. In the January raid alone, agents arrested approximately 3,000 people in 33 cities in a single night. Many were held without charge; some were deported without trial. The most prominent deportee was the anarchist Emma Goldman, who was sent to Russia in December 1919.

The raids were eventually condemned by legal experts and civil liberties groups. In May 1920, a group of twelve eminent lawyers published a report describing them as a systematic violation of constitutional rights. Palmer’s credibility collapsed when his predicted uprising on 1 May 1920 failed to materialise. The raids were significant, however, in linking immigration, radicalism and foreignness in the public mind — a connection that shaped the immigration restrictions of the 1920s.

In April 1920, a paymaster and a security guard were murdered during a robbery at a shoe factory in South Braintree, Massachusetts. Two Italian-born anarchists, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were arrested and charged with the murders. Both men denied the charges but were convicted in July 1921 after a trial widely criticised for bias: witnesses who provided alibis were dismissed, and the judge made prejudicial remarks about the defendants’ anarchist beliefs and foreign origins.

The case became an international cause. Protests were held across Europe and Latin America. Intellectuals and writers condemned the trial as a miscarriage of justice rooted in anti-immigrant prejudice and anti-anarchist hysteria. After several appeals failed, Sacco and Vanzetti were executed on 23 August 1927. Their case remains the most famous symbol of American nativism and the dangers of political prejudice in the justice system during the 1920s. Massachusetts officially acknowledged in 1977 that they had not received a fair trial.

The United States as a Nation of Contrasts

The immigration restrictions of the 1920s reveal one of the deepest contradictions in American life. The United States had built its wealth and identity on immigration, yet it moved decisively to close the door — driven by racial prejudice, economic anxiety and political fear. For millions of would-be immigrants, the American dream became inaccessible. For those who were already there, the Red Scare and the Sacco and Vanzetti case showed how quickly rights could be stripped away when fear and prejudice dominated public life.

lesson_title: Religion and race: the Bible Belt and the KKK
content_html:
Religious Fundamentalism and the Bible Belt

In many parts of rural America, particularly across the southern and mid-western states, Protestant Christianity was more than a private belief — it shaped schooling, politics and daily life. This region, stretching from Texas to Virginia, became known as the Bible Belt. For religious fundamentalists, the Bible was the literal word of God, to be accepted without question. Darwin’s theory of evolution was seen as a direct challenge to the Biblical account of creation in Genesis.

The conflict between religion and modern science exploded into public view in 1925. Tennessee had passed the Butler Act that year, making it illegal to teach evolution in state-funded schools. A young biology teacher named John Scopes deliberately challenged the law by teaching evolution to his class in Dayton, Tennessee. His arrest and trial became a national sensation.

Key Fact

The 1925 Scopes Trial in Dayton, Tennessee, pitted William Jennings Bryan (fundamentalist) against Clarence Darrow (defence) over the teaching of evolution. Scopes was convicted and fined $100, but the trial exposed fundamentalism to national ridicule and was broadcast live on radio to millions of Americans.

The prosecution was led by William Jennings Bryan, a three-time presidential candidate and devout fundamentalist. The defence was led by Clarence Darrow, one of the most famous lawyers in America. The trial became a clash of worldviews: Bryan argued that the Bible must govern what was taught in schools; Darrow argued that freedom of thought and scientific inquiry must not be sacrificed to religious doctrine.

Scopes was convicted and fined $100 (the verdict was later overturned on a technicality). However, the real verdict went to the modernists. Broadcast live on radio, the trial allowed millions to hear Darrow cross-examine Bryan directly on the Bible — an embarrassing experience for Bryan, who struggled to answer questions about the age of the Earth. Bryan died five days after the trial ended. Although fundamentalism did not disappear, its influence on national politics weakened after 1925.

Segregation and Jim Crow

For African Americans, the 1920s were years of profound inequality. Across the South, Jim Crow laws enforced the separation of Black and white Americans in schools, transport, restaurants, hospitals and courtrooms. The 1896 Supreme Court decision in Plessy v. Ferguson had declared “separate but equal” facilities constitutional, providing legal cover for systematic discrimination.

In practice, Black facilities were rarely equal. Schools for Black children received a fraction of the funding allocated to white schools. Voting rights were suppressed through poll taxes, literacy tests and the constant threat of violence. Lynching — the murder of Black people, usually by hanging, by white mobs — was used as a weapon of terror. Between 1882 and 1968, approximately 3,446 Black Americans were lynched, according to records compiled by the NAACP. The 1920s saw a peak of racial violence, including the Tulsa Race Massacre of 1921, in which a prosperous Black neighbourhood was destroyed by a white mob.

Key Fact

The revived Ku Klux Klan, re-founded in 1915, reached a peak membership of approximately 4–5 million by the mid-1920s. Unlike the original post-Civil War Klan, the 1920s Klan targeted not only Black Americans but also Catholics, Jews, immigrants and trade unionists, and had significant political influence in several states.

The Rebirth of the Ku Klux Klan

The original Ku Klux Klan was founded in the South after the Civil War to terrorise newly freed Black Americans. It was largely suppressed by the 1870s. In 1915, it was revived by William Joseph Simmons at Stone Mountain, Georgia, partly inspired by the racist film The Birth of a Nation. The 1920s Klan was a mass movement, not just a fringe organisation. It attracted millions of members across the North and Midwest as well as the South, appealing to working-class white Protestants who felt threatened by immigration, urbanisation and social change.

The Klan used terror — beatings, arson and murder — but also operated openly through marches, political endorsements and church events. By 1924 it had significant influence in the Democratic Party’s national convention. Its power declined sharply after 1925, when a prominent Klan leader, David Stephenson, was convicted of the murder of a young woman in Indiana. The scandal drove many members away. However, the Klan’s violence had already caused immense harm.

African Americans organised to resist racism in different ways. The NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People), founded in 1909, campaigned through legal challenges and lobbying for anti-lynching legislation. Although Congress blocked an anti-lynching bill in the 1920s, the NAACP kept pressure on lawmakers and publicised racial violence to northern audiences.

Marcus Garvey offered a different vision. His UNIA (Universal Negro Improvement Association) promoted Black pride, economic self-help and, ultimately, the idea that African Americans should return to Africa to build an independent nation. Garvey attracted hundreds of thousands of followers, particularly in urban Black communities. He was imprisoned in 1925 on fraud charges and deported in 1927, but his ideas influenced later Black nationalist movements.

The most significant response to southern racism was migration. In the Great Migration, approximately 1.6 million Black Americans moved north and west between 1910 and 1930, seeking factory work in cities like Chicago, Detroit and New York, and escaping the worst of Jim Crow segregation. This migration created vibrant Black urban communities and was the foundation of the Harlem Renaissance.

content_html:
Why Prohibition Was Introduced

On 16 January 1920, Prohibition came into force across the United States. The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified in January 1919, was supported by a powerful coalition of social reformers, religious groups and temperance campaigners who argued that alcohol destroyed families, fuelled crime and reduced industrial productivity. The Women’s Christian Temperance Union and the Anti-Saloon League had lobbied Congress for decades.

The timing of Prohibition was shaped by the First World War. The large number of German-American families who owned breweries gave temperance campaigners a patriotic argument: banning alcohol would hurt German immigrants and free up grain for the war effort. The Volstead Act of October 1919 defined the beverages covered by the amendment and gave the federal government the power to enforce the ban.

Key Fact

Prohibition began on 16 January 1920 under the Eighteenth Amendment, enforced by the Volstead Act. It was supported by temperance groups, religious organisations and some progressives who believed alcohol was a social evil. It lasted until the Twenty-First Amendment ended it in December 1933.

Life Under Prohibition: Speakeasies and Bootleggers

Prohibition did not stop Americans drinking — it drove the trade underground. Speakeasies sprang up in every major city. Estimates suggest that by the late 1920s there were around 30,000 speakeasies in New York City alone — more than double the number of legal bars before Prohibition. Customers needed a password to enter, and owners bribed police officers to look the other way.

Bootlegging — the illegal manufacture and sale of alcohol — became enormously profitable. Criminals who had previously run small-scale operations now controlled vast networks for importing, manufacturing and distributing spirits and beer. Alcohol was smuggled across the Canadian and Mexican borders and brewed illegally in private stills known as “moonshine” operations. The profits from bootlegging bankrolled the rise of organised crime in American cities.

No figure better symbolised organised crime during Prohibition than Al Capone. Born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1899, Capone moved to Chicago and by the mid-1920s controlled the city’s illegal alcohol trade. His gang, known as the Chicago Outfit, earned an estimated $60 million per year at its peak — equivalent to hundreds of millions in today’s money. Capone’s operations covered bootlegging, gambling, prostitution and extortion. He employed over 600 gunmen and routinely bribed police officers, judges and local politicians.

On 14 February 1929, members of Capone’s gang, dressed as police officers, murdered seven members of a rival gang in a Chicago garage. The St Valentine's Day Massacre shocked even a public accustomed to gang violence. It illustrated how completely Prohibition had empowered criminal organisations. Despite being widely blamed, Capone was never charged with the murders. He was eventually convicted in October 1931 of tax evasion and sentenced to eleven years in prison.

Key Fact

The St Valentine’s Day Massacre took place on 14 February 1929. Seven members of the Bugs Moran gang were killed in Chicago, widely attributed to Capone’s organisation. It demonstrated the lethal power of criminal syndicates that Prohibition had created and helped turn public opinion against the Eighteenth Amendment.

Political Corruption: Harding and the Ohio Gang

Organised crime could not have flourished without political corruption. President Warren G. Harding, elected in 1920, surrounded himself with cronies from Ohio who used their positions for personal gain — a group known as the Ohio Gang. Harding himself was not shown to be personally corrupt in the major scandals, but his administration was riddled with dishonesty.

The most damaging scandal was the Teapot Dome Scandal. Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased government oil reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, and Elk Hills, California, to private oil companies in exchange for cash bribes totalling around $400,000. Fall became the first United States Cabinet member to be convicted of a crime committed while in office. Harding died in August 1923, before the full scale of the corruption was revealed, but his presidency is remembered as one of the most corrupt in American history.

Prohibition failed for several interconnected reasons. The federal government employed only around 1,500 Prohibition agents to police the entire country — a hopelessly small force that was also poorly paid and therefore vulnerable to bribery. Enforcement was inconsistent: in rural areas, especially in the South, Prohibition was often accepted; in major cities it was widely defied.

The profits from bootlegging were so enormous that criminal gangs could afford to bribe almost anyone who stood in their way. Public opinion also shifted over the decade. Many Americans who had initially supported Prohibition came to see it as an infringement of personal liberty that had simply created a more dangerous society. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 provided the final push — legalising alcohol would create jobs and generate tax revenue for a struggling government. The Twenty-First Amendment, which repealed Prohibition, was ratified in December 1933.
