content_html:
America’s Economic Starting Point

In 1910, the United States was already the world’s largest industrial economy. It had vast natural resources — coal, iron, oil and timber — spread across a continental territory larger than most European nations combined. A large and growing domestic market meant that American manufacturers could produce at scale. The country had already built a dense network of railroads that connected raw materials, factories and consumers.

These advantages gave the United States a head start when the First World War began in 1914. While European economies tore themselves apart, American businesses supplied both sides with weapons, food, chemicals and manufactured goods. By 1917, when the United States entered the war, American banks had lent billions of dollars to the Allied powers. When the war ended in 1918, Europe was physically devastated and financially exhausted; the United States was the world’s leading creditor nation.

Key Fact

By 1920 the United States produced approximately 40 per cent of the world’s manufactured goods. The First World War accelerated this dominance by destroying European industrial capacity while American factories profited from wartime orders. The United States also became Europe’s largest creditor, with massive loans to Britain and France.

Mass Production: Henry Ford and the Assembly Line

The most powerful engine of the 1920s boom was mass production. Henry Ford had introduced the moving assembly line at his Highland Park plant in 1913, revolutionising manufacturing. By breaking production into simple, repetitive tasks, Ford could build a Model T car every 93 minutes by 1914. The cost of a Model T fell from $825 in 1908 to $260 by 1925, bringing car ownership within reach of ordinary workers.

The car industry did not just sell cars — it created demand for steel, rubber, glass, leather, oil and road construction. Economists estimate that by the late 1920s the automobile industry was driving around one in nine jobs in the United States. The spread of car ownership transformed American life: suburbs expanded, roadside businesses multiplied, and the country became more mobile and connected.

Electrification powered a consumer revolution. By 1929, around 70 per cent of American homes had electricity, compared with much lower rates in Europe. The growing power grid enabled mass production of electrical appliances — refrigerators, washing machines, vacuum cleaners and radios — that transformed domestic life. Companies like General Electric and Westinghouse expanded rapidly to meet demand.

The result was a self-reinforcing cycle: higher productivity in factories meant lower prices; lower prices meant more consumers could afford goods; more consumers meant higher output; higher output meant more factory workers with wages to spend. This virtuous circle defined the 1920s boom. Total consumer spending in the United States grew from approximately $48 billion in 1919 to nearly $79 billion by 1929.

Key Fact

Hire purchase (buying on credit) fuelled the consumer boom by allowing Americans to buy goods they could not afford outright. By the late 1920s, around 60 per cent of all cars and 80 per cent of all radios were bought on credit. This extended the boom but also left many households heavily in debt.

Republican Economics: Laissez-Faire and Protectionism

The Republican administrations of the 1920s — under Presidents Harding, Coolidge and Hoover — followed a philosophy of laissez-faire economics. The government cut income taxes for the wealthy, reduced business regulation, and refused to regulate the financial sector. The belief was that what was good for big business was good for America — often summarised in President Coolidge’s remark that “the chief business of the American people is business.”

Alongside laissez-faire, the Republicans pursued economic protectionism. The Fordney–McCumber Tariff of 1922 raised import duties to their highest level since the Civil War, protecting American manufacturers from cheaper European goods. In the short term, this benefited American industry; in the longer term, it damaged international trade and contributed to the fragility that made the Great Depression so severe.

The 1920s boom was real, but it was deeply unequal. Farmers did not share in the prosperity. During the First World War, agricultural prices had been high because of demand from Europe. When European farming recovered after 1918, American farm prices collapsed. Throughout the 1920s, millions of farmers — particularly in the South and Midwest — struggled with low prices, debt and foreclosures. By 1929, roughly half of all Americans still lived in rural areas, and most of them were not experiencing the “Roaring Twenties.”

Black Americans, recent immigrants and unskilled industrial workers also benefited little from the boom. Wages for unskilled workers rose more slowly than profits. The top 5 per cent of income earners received approximately one-third of all personal income in the United States in 1929. This concentration of wealth at the top and the over-reliance on credit created the conditions for the economic collapse that followed.

unit_name: The USA: A Nation of Contrasts, 1910-1929
lesson_title: The end of prosperity: the Wall Street Crash, 1929
content_html:
The Seeds of Collapse: Overproduction and Underconsumption

Even as the 1920s boom appeared to be at its height, deep structural weaknesses were developing beneath the surface. The most fundamental was the gap between what American factories could produce and what consumers could afford to buy. Overproduction had been building throughout the decade. Factories, driven by mass production techniques, could turn out goods at a rate that outstripped real demand. Once hire purchase credit was exhausted and storage warehouses filled up, factories began cutting production — and with cuts in production came lay-offs and falling wages.

This problem was made worse by the unequal distribution of wealth. The top 5 per cent of Americans received roughly one-third of all personal income in 1929, while tens of millions of farmers, unskilled workers and Black Americans had little disposable income. When factories produced consumer goods in vast quantities, there was a finite number of people who could afford to buy them, even on credit. Falling agricultural incomes meant that the rural half of the population was a weak consumer base throughout the decade.

Key Fact

By the late 1920s, American manufacturers were producing more goods than consumers could buy. Unsold goods piled up in warehouses. Companies began cutting output and laying off workers, reducing consumer purchasing power further — a downward spiral that made the economy increasingly fragile before the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.

Speculation and the Stock Market Bubble

While the productive economy was showing signs of strain, the stock market was booming. Throughout the 1920s, rising share prices attracted millions of ordinary Americans into the stock market for the first time. Between 1920 and 1929, share prices on the New York Stock Exchange roughly tripled. The belief that share prices would always rise encouraged reckless speculation.

The most dangerous practice was buying on the margin. Investors typically paid only 10 per cent of a share’s price upfront, borrowing the rest from their stockbroker. This worked brilliantly when prices rose — investors could sell at a profit and repay the loan. But if prices fell, the broker could demand immediate repayment of the loan (a “margin call”), forcing investors to sell shares at a loss. The entire system depended on prices continuing to rise.

The Wall Street Crash was not the first speculative collapse of the decade. Between 1924 and 1926, a land speculation boom in Florida drew hundreds of thousands of investors. Property prices in Miami doubled, then doubled again, as speculators bought and resold plots of land at rising prices without any intention of building on them. The boom collapsed in 1926, partly because of a devastating hurricane that killed approximately 400 people. Millions of investors lost their money. The Florida collapse was a warning of what happened when asset prices lost touch with underlying value — a warning that went unheeded on Wall Street.

Key Fact

Black Thursday fell on 24 October 1929. Around 12.9 million shares were sold in a single day as investors panicked. On “Black Tuesday” five days later, on 29 October 1929, over 16 million shares were traded, and the market collapsed catastrophically. Billions of dollars of paper wealth were wiped out within days.

The Crash: Panic Selling and Market Collapse

By September 1929, share prices had begun to slide. Nervous investors started selling. As prices fell, margin calls went out to investors who had borrowed to buy shares; to pay their debts, they sold more shares, pushing prices down further. The Wall Street Crash was self-reinforcing — falling prices caused selling which caused further price falls.

On 24 October 1929 — Black Thursday — approximately 12.9 million shares changed hands as panic spread. Leading bankers temporarily steadied prices by purchasing shares, but the recovery was brief. On 29 October — Black Tuesday — more than 16 million shares were traded in a single day, and prices collapsed. By mid-November 1929, share prices had fallen by approximately 40 per cent from their September peak. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which had reached 381 points in September 1929, eventually bottomed out at 41 points in July 1932 — a fall of nearly 90 per cent from its peak.

The Crash did not cause the Great Depression on its own — it triggered a crisis whose roots lay in overproduction, agricultural decline, unequal wealth distribution and weak banking regulation. As share prices collapsed, banks that had lent money for stock speculation faced ruin; many called in loans to businesses, which then cut production and laid off workers. Consumer spending collapsed as millions became unemployed. By 1933, approximately 13 million Americans — around 25 per cent of the workforce — were unemployed, and thousands of banks had failed.

The international consequences were equally severe. American banks recalled loans to European countries, pushing Germany and other fragile economies into depression. World trade collapsed as countries raised tariffs against each other. The “Roaring Twenties” ended not with a gradual fading but with a catastrophic collapse that transformed the economic and political landscape of the Western world for the next decade.

unit_name: The USA: A Nation of Contrasts, 1910-1929
lesson_title: Popular entertainment in the Jazz Age
content_html:
Hollywood and the Silent Movie Era

The 1920s transformed entertainment in the United States, creating a mass popular culture that had never existed before. At the centre of this transformation was the cinema. By the early 1920s, going to the pictures was the most popular leisure activity in America, with approximately 80 million cinema tickets sold every week by 1929 — in a country with a total population of around 120 million. Hollywood had become synonymous with glamour, escapism and modernity.

Silent films had been entertaining audiences since the 1890s, but the 1920s produced the first true film stars whose fame was genuinely national. Charlie Chaplin, whose “Tramp” character was recognised across America and around the world, became one of the highest-paid performers of the decade. Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and Rudolph Valentino were household names. The arrival of the talkies in 1927 revolutionised the industry all over again.

Key Fact

The first major “talkie” was The Jazz Singer, released in October 1927, starring Al Jolson. Within two years, silent films had almost completely disappeared. Talkies gave Hollywood a new commercial advantage: English-language dialogue made American films especially influential in Britain and other English-speaking markets.

Cinema did more than entertain — it spread a common culture across a vast and diverse nation. Movie stars set fashion trends that millions of women copied. Fans wrote to studios in their thousands, creating the world’s first celebrity culture on an industrial scale. For many immigrants and rural Americans who had moved to cities, cinema was an affordable and accessible window onto a glamorous world far removed from their daily lives.

Cinema also attracted controversy. Religious groups and social conservatives worried about the moral messages of some films — particularly those that showed women in revealing clothing, portrayed extramarital romance, or glorified crime. In 1922, the film industry appointed Will Hays to clean up Hollywood’s image. The “Hays Code” of the early 1930s would eventually introduce strict censorship, but during the 1920s films remained relatively uncensored and controversial.

Jazz: The Music of the Age

Jazz was the music that gave the 1920s its nickname. Originating in African American communities in New Orleans, jazz combined blues, ragtime and improvisation to create music that was spontaneous, rhythmic and irresistibly danceable. By the early 1920s, jazz had spread from New Orleans up the Mississippi to Chicago and New York, carried by African American musicians including Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington.

Louis Armstrong, who moved from New Orleans to Chicago in 1922, became the most celebrated jazz musician of the decade. His trumpet playing and improvisational style defined what jazz sounded like. Duke Ellington brought jazz to the prestigious Cotton Club in Harlem, New York, where from 1927 onwards his orchestra played to wealthy audiences and was broadcast nationally on radio. The Harlem Renaissance produced not just music but poetry, visual art and literature that challenged racial stereotypes and demanded recognition of Black Americans’ cultural contributions.

Key Fact

The Harlem Renaissance was a flourishing of African American culture centred in Harlem, New York, during the 1920s. Duke Ellington’s Cotton Club residency from 1927 was broadcast nationally on radio, introducing jazz to millions of white Americans and making it the defining sound of the Jazz Age. Jazz was controversial: many conservatives condemned it as immoral and associated with Black culture.

Radio, the Gramophone and Mass Media

The spread of radio was one of the most dramatic changes of the decade. The first commercial radio station in the United States, KDKA in Pittsburgh, began broadcasting in November 1920. By 1929, there were approximately 600 radio stations in America and over 10 million radio sets in American homes. For the first time, millions of people could hear the same news, the same music and the same sporting events simultaneously — a revolution in shared national experience.

Radio and the gramophone together drove the commercial popularisation of jazz. Record sales boomed in the early 1920s; by 1927, Americans were buying approximately 100 million records a year. Jazz, popular songs and classical music all competed for listeners. The gramophone brought professional-quality music into working-class homes that could never have afforded concert tickets. Dancing to recorded music became a new social activity, and the Charleston dance craze of 1923 swept across the country.

Speakeasies — the illegal bars of the Prohibition era — were important cultural spaces as well as criminal enterprises. Many speakeasies featured jazz bands and dance floors, and they were among the few spaces where Black and white Americans could socialise together. In this sense, Prohibition inadvertently created the conditions for a blurring of racial boundaries that the rest of 1920s society vigorously maintained. The speakeasy also became closely associated with the flapper lifestyle — young women who dressed in short skirts, cut their hair short, wore make-up and drank and smoked publicly in defiance of social convention.

unit_name: The USA: A Nation of Contrasts, 1910-1929
content_html:
Women Before the First World War

In 1910, the lives of most American women were shaped by narrow social expectations. Married middle-class women were expected to manage the home and raise children. Working-class women often laboured in factories or domestic service but had no political voice. Women could not vote in federal elections. The suffrage movement had been campaigning since the 1840s, winning the vote in some western states, but federal suffrage remained elusive. Alongside the suffrage campaign, progressive women were active in social reform — campaigning against child labour, for better working conditions and for public health improvements.

The progressive era (roughly 1890 to 1920) saw women take on expanding public roles. Organisations such as the Women’s Christian Temperance Union gave women a platform for political action outside formal politics. Women like Jane Addams, founder of Hull House in Chicago, pioneered social work and urban reform. By 1910, women were already in the workforce in significant numbers — as teachers, nurses, secretaries and factory workers — though they were systematically paid less than men.

Key Fact

The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified on 18 August 1920, gave women the right to vote in all federal elections. It was a major political landmark, the result of seventy years of campaigning. However, it did not remove racial barriers: Black women in the South were systematically prevented from voting by the same Jim Crow laws and intimidation that blocked Black men.

The First World War and Women’s Work

The entry of the United States into the First World War in April 1917 opened new opportunities for women. With millions of men in uniform, women moved into jobs previously closed to them: working in munitions factories, on the railways and in offices. Approximately 11,000 women served in the US Navy in non-combat roles. This direct contribution to the war effort strengthened the argument that women deserved the vote. When the war ended, many women were pushed out of their wartime jobs as returning soldiers reclaimed them, but the experience of wartime work had permanently changed expectations.

The most iconic image of the 1920s woman was the flapper. Flappers were typically young, urban and middle-class. They wore short skirts (above the knee), cut their hair in a short “bob,” wore make-up, smoked cigarettes and drank cocktails in speakeasies. They danced the Charleston and the Black Bottom. They drove cars and attended college in increasing numbers. The flapper represented a deliberate rejection of the Victorian ideal of the modest, domestic “angel in the house.”

Jazz culture was central to the flapper lifestyle. The speakeasy, the cinema, the radio and the gramophone all gave young women new social spaces and new freedoms. Hollywood glamorised the flapper image through films starring actresses like Clara Bow, who was marketed as the “It Girl” and became one of the biggest stars of the decade. Fashion magazines spread the flapper look nationwide.

Key Fact

The flapper lifestyle represented real but limited change. It was largely restricted to young, urban, white, middle-class women. The majority of American women — working-class, rural, Black, immigrant — did not live like flappers. Most women still worked in low-paid domestic or clerical jobs and faced significant inequality in wages and career opportunities.

Margaret Sanger and Birth Control

One of the most controversial women of the decade was Margaret Sanger. Sanger had been campaigning for women’s access to birth control since the 1910s, arguing that women could not be truly free until they could control their own reproduction. She founded the American Birth Control League in 1921, which later became Planned Parenthood. Her work was controversial: contraception was still illegal in many states, and she was prosecuted multiple times. However, by the late 1920s, birth control clinics were operating in several major cities, and middle-class women were increasingly able to access contraception.

The changes in women’s lives during the 1920s provoked strong reactions. Religious fundamentalists and conservative commentators condemned flappers as immoral and dangerous to family life. Many states considered legislation to restrict short skirts or bobbed hair. The Ku Klux Klan explicitly campaigned to return women to their “proper place” in the home. Some women themselves were critical of the flapper, arguing that it prioritised fashion and pleasure over serious feminist goals.

By 1930, many of the freedoms associated with the flapper had retreated. The Great Depression made survival a priority; spending on fashion and entertainment collapsed; and conservative social attitudes reasserted themselves. Women were urged to give up jobs to men. The 1920s represented a partial and uneven change: significant for those who lived through it, but far from a complete revolution in women’s status.

content_html:
The Legacy of the Reservation System

By 1910, the fate of Native American peoples had already been largely determined by a century of displacement and conquest. The reservation system had forced the majority of Native Americans onto parcels of land that were often arid, economically marginal and isolated from markets and services. Tribes had been stripped of vast territories through a combination of military force, broken treaties and legal manipulation. The buffalo herds that had sustained Plains cultures had been deliberately hunted to near-extinction in the 1870s and 1880s.

Into this already diminished world, the Dawes Act of 1887 brought further devastation. The law broke up communally held tribal land into individual allotments — 160 acres per family — and sold the “surplus” land to white settlers. Between 1887 and 1934, Native Americans lost approximately 90 million acres of their remaining land — about two-thirds of what they had held in 1887. The allotment system destroyed the communal economic and social structures on which tribal life depended, without providing meaningful support for individual farming.

Key Fact

The Dawes Act of 1887 broke up communal tribal lands into individual allotments and sold the remaining land to white settlers. Between 1887 and 1934, Native Americans lost approximately 90 million acres — roughly two-thirds of their 1887 land holdings. By 1910, most reservations were poverty-stricken, with inadequate schools, healthcare and economic opportunities.

Native American Boarding Schools

The US government’s official policy towards Native Americans in this period was forced assimilation. The most direct tool of assimilation was the Native American boarding school system. The most famous was the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania, founded in 1879. The philosophy behind these schools was summed up in the school’s founder Richard Henry Pratt’s phrase: “Kill the Indian, save the man.”

Children were taken from their families — sometimes by force — and transported to schools hundreds of miles away. At school they were forbidden to speak their native languages, wear traditional clothing or practise their religions. Their hair was cut. They were given English names. Punishments for speaking native languages could be severe. Death rates in boarding schools were high, partly from disease in crowded conditions, partly from inadequate care. By the early twentieth century, thousands of Native American children were passing through this system each year.

The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) was responsible for administering reservations and the boarding school system. Throughout the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the BIA was plagued by corruption and incompetence. Agents who managed reservations often enriched themselves at the expense of the tribes they were supposed to serve. Food, medicine and resources allocated to reservations were frequently siphoned off. Congress periodically investigated scandals but effective reform was slow to materialise.

The 1928 Meriam Report, commissioned by the government, documented the catastrophic conditions on reservations in detail: extreme poverty, malnutrition, high disease rates, inadequate schools, and the failures of the Dawes allotment system. Its findings eventually contributed to the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 under President Franklin Roosevelt, which reversed the allotment policy. But through the 1910s and 1920s, conditions remained dire.

Key Fact

The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 granted US citizenship to all Native Americans born in the United States. This was partly in recognition of the 12,000 Native Americans who had served in the US military during the First World War. However, citizenship did not automatically give Native Americans the right to vote in all states — several states maintained laws blocking them from voting well into the 1940s and beyond.

The Indian Citizenship Act, 1924

In 1924, Congress passed the Indian Citizenship Act, granting US citizenship to all Native Americans born within the borders of the United States. It was a significant symbolic recognition, partly prompted by the service of approximately 12,000 Native Americans in the First World War, many of them volunteers. Some Native Americans and their advocates welcomed it as a step towards equal rights. Others were deeply ambivalent: citizenship had not been asked for, came with conditions that undermined tribal sovereignty, and in several states did not translate into the right to vote.

While Wall Street boomed and flappers danced, conditions on most reservations barely changed. The majority of Native Americans lived in deep poverty, with life expectancy significantly below the national average. Unemployment on reservations was chronic. Access to healthcare and education was minimal by national standards. The federal government’s assimilation policy had failed on its own terms — it had destroyed traditional economies without successfully integrating Native Americans into the mainstream economy. The 1920s boom is a particularly stark illustration of the “nation of contrasts” theme: the most prosperous decade in American history to that point was, for Native Americans, simply another decade of dispossession and neglect.

content_html:
Was the 1920s a “Roaring” Decade?

The phrase “Roaring Twenties” has shaped how the decade is remembered — as a time of prosperity, jazz, Hollywood glamour and social freedom. But historians have long debated how far this image reflects the experience of all Americans. The title of the unit — “A Nation of Contrasts” — is itself a historical claim: that the 1920s United States was defined by a dramatic gap between prosperity and poverty, freedom and oppression, modernity and tradition. This lesson examines that claim through the lens of different historical historical interpretations.

Historians have interpreted the 1920s in sharply different ways. Some contemporary observers and later popular historians emphasised the decade’s energy and dynamism — Frederick Lewis Allen’s famous 1931 account Only Yesterday captured the excitement of the decade as he had lived through it, focusing on flappers, jazz, cinema and the stock market boom. But historians writing from the 1960s onwards, including Lynn Dumenil, offered a more complex picture: one in which cultural anxiety, racial violence and economic inequality ran alongside and often contradicted the glamorous surface.

Key Fact

Frederick Lewis Allen’s Only Yesterday (1931) presented the 1920s as a decade of social liberation and economic optimism. Lynn Dumenil’s The Modern Temper (1995) argued that the decade was equally characterised by cultural conflict, racial violence, nativist anxiety and the fragility of prosperity. These two interpretations represent the core debate about the decade’s real character.

The Rural–Urban Divide

One of the most important contrasts was geographical. The “Roaring Twenties” was primarily an urban experience. New York, Chicago and Los Angeles had cinemas, speakeasies, jazz clubs and department stores selling the latest consumer goods. But by 1929, roughly half of all Americans still lived in rural areas, and many of them were not sharing in the prosperity. Farmers across the South and Midwest had suffered from chronically low agricultural prices throughout the decade, following the collapse of wartime demand in 1918. Farm bankruptcies and foreclosures were common throughout the 1920s — the decade’s “boom” was, for rural America, already a prolonged depression.

The fundamentalist versus modernist conflict — illustrated by the Scopes Trial of 1925 — was also a rural-urban divide. Rural, Protestant, conservative America looked with suspicion and hostility at the jazz, the cinema and the flappers of the cities. The Ku Klux Klan, reaching 4–5 million members in the mid-1920s, drew its strength from precisely those communities that felt left behind by the urban boom.

The Sacco and Vanzetti case (1920–1927) is one of the most powerful pieces of evidence for the “nation of contrasts” interpretation. Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti were Italian-born anarchists convicted of murder in a trial that critics worldwide condemned as a miscarriage of justice rooted in anti-immigrant prejudice and anti-anarchist hysteria. They were executed on 23 August 1927 — at almost precisely the decade’s midpoint — despite international protests. Massachusetts officially acknowledged in 1977 that they had not received a fair trial.

The case illustrates a paradox at the heart of the 1920s. The United States celebrated itself as a land of freedom and opportunity; yet its justice system was shown to be capable of executing men on the basis of their ethnicity and political beliefs. For historians who argue that the decade was a “nation of contrasts,” Sacco and Vanzetti represent what lay beneath the glittering surface of the Jazz Age.

Key Fact

The “nation of contrasts” interpretation holds that the prosperity of the 1920s was real but deeply unequal. The strongest evidence: the KKK reaching 4–5 million members while jazz spread nationally; Native American reservation poverty alongside Wall Street’s boom; the Sacco and Vanzetti case exposing prejudice in the justice system; and farmers in depression while urban consumers bought on credit.

Why Do Interpretations of the 1920s Differ?

Understanding why historical historical interpretations of the 1920s differ is as important as knowing what those interpretations say. Allen wrote Only Yesterday in 1931, just two years after the Crash, using his own memories and journalism. He was an educated, urban, white American who had lived through the boom personally — his perspective naturally emphasised the decade’s vitality.

Dumenil, writing in 1995, had access to decades of subsequent scholarship — including social history, African American history, labour history and women’s history — that had dramatically expanded what historians knew about who was excluded from the boom. She also wrote after the civil rights movement and feminist scholarship had made racial and gender inequality central to American historical consciousness. These differences in time of writing, sources used, questions asked and the author’s own standpoint all explain why interpretations differ.

The most common error on the 10-mark “Compare Interpretations” question is to explain how two interpretations differ (what each says) rather than why they differ. Examiners award top marks for explaining the reasons behind the differences: the author’s purpose, the time at which they were writing, the evidence they used, and their own standpoint or background. For the 1920s, a strong answer might note that Allen wrote as a contemporary observer using personal memory, while Dumenil had access to sixty years of additional social and racial history scholarship. This explains why one emphasises dynamism and the other emphasises conflict and inequality.

When evaluating an interpretation with a 12-mark question, you must both agree and disagree, using your own contextual knowledge — not just summarise what each historian says. A top-band answer agrees that the decade was prosperous for many but uses evidence of KKK growth, farm poverty, Sacco-Vanzetti and reservation conditions to challenge any one-sided reading of the decade as simply “roaring.”

content_html:
Understanding the Exam Paper

This unit is examined through a mix of source-based questions, interpretation questions and extended essay questions. Understanding exactly what each question type demands is as important as knowing your content. This lesson brings together the skills you have been developing across the unit — source utility, comparing interpretations, explaining causes and consequences, and arguing in extended essays — and shows you how to apply them under exam conditions.

Exam questions on this unit will draw on the full range of topics: immigration and the Red Scare, religion and race, Prohibition and organised crime, the economic boom, the Wall Street Crash, popular entertainment, women’s changing roles, Native Americans and the “nation of contrasts” debate. The skills tested change by question type, so you need to know which skill each question is testing — and resist the temptation to write everything you know.

Key Fact

A top-band source utility answer must combine three elements: content (what the source actually says or shows), provenance (who produced it, when, why and for what audience) and contextual knowledge (what you know from your own study that confirms or challenges the source). Mentioning only provenance — “it is biased because Capone had a reason to lie” — is the most common error and will cap you at the lower mark bands.

Applying Source Utility: The Five-Step Method

When answering a source utility question, follow these five steps. First, identify the specific enquiry the question asks about — “useful for finding out about…” requires a specific focus. Second, examine what the source content tells you directly. Third, analyse the provenance: who made it, when, why and for whom. Fourth, use your contextual knowledge to confirm or challenge the source — does what you know from your study support or limit what the source shows? Fifth, make an overall judgement about the extent of the source’s usefulness.

Consider a typical source for this unit: a Ku Klux Klan recruitment poster from the mid-1920s. The content tells you what the Klan said it stood for — “100% American,” Protestantism, anti-immigration. The provenance tells you it was created by the Klan to recruit members — so it presents the most attractive version of the Klan’s message and omits its violence and corruption. Your contextual knowledge tells you that: the Klan reached 4–5 million members by the mid-1920s (confirming that the appeal was real); that it used terror, murder and arson (challenging any impression that it was simply a patriotic organisation); and that its appeal drew on nativist fears of immigration, urbanisation and racial mixing.

Consider a cartoon published in a temperance organisation’s newspaper in 1921, showing a father spending his wages on drink while his children starve. This source might be useful for an enquiry into why Prohibition was introduced — its content shows the temperance argument that alcohol destroys family life; its provenance (temperance publication) means it presents the anti-alcohol case in its strongest form and will omit evidence of the harms caused by Prohibition itself; your contextual knowledge tells you that the Women’s Christian Temperance Union and the Anti-Saloon League did genuinely argue for Prohibition on exactly these grounds, supporting the source’s usefulness for understanding the case for the ban.

The same source would be much less useful for an enquiry into whether Prohibition succeeded, because: (a) it was produced by Prohibition supporters before the problems were known; (b) its purpose was propaganda, not neutral reporting; and (c) your contextual knowledge shows that Prohibition spectacularly failed to stop drinking, creating speakeasies and organised crime instead. A strong utility answer always specifies the enquiry and adjusts the assessment accordingly.

Key Fact

On a “Compare Interpretations” question, the top mark band requires you to explain why interpretations differ. The three main reasons are: time of writing (when was the historian writing, and what did they know?); sources used (what evidence did they draw on?); and purpose and standpoint (who was the historian, and why were they writing this?). Simply describing what each interpretation says is the mid-band response.

Writing the Extended Essay: Structure and Technique

Extended essay questions — whether 12-mark “How far do you agree” or 16-mark “How far… / Account for…” — reward clear structure, specific evidence and a substantiated overall judgement. The most common mistake is describing two sides without reaching a conclusion. Examiners specifically look for a judgment that goes beyond “both sides have merit” — you need to say which side is more convincing, and why, backed by evidence.

Use the following structure for extended essays. First, a brief introduction that signals your overall argument — do you agree, partly agree or disagree? Second, paragraphs that develop points in favour of the statement, each with specific evidence. Third, paragraphs that develop points against the statement or in favour of an alternative argument, each with specific evidence. Fourth, a conclusion that reaches and justifies your overall judgement. The StudyVault rubric for extended essays describes top-band responses (Mastering) as having “a sophisticated argument with embedded evidence and sustained analysis.”

The strongest extended essay answers draw on multiple topics from the unit rather than treating each lesson as a separate silo. For a question about whether the United States truly was a “nation of contrasts,” the top-band answer would connect: immigration restriction and the Red Scare (fear and prejudice); the KKK and Jim Crow (racial violence); farm poverty alongside Wall Street boom (economic inequality); Native American reservation poverty alongside consumer culture; Sacco and Vanzetti’s execution alongside democratic ideals; flappers’ limited freedom alongside the continued exclusion of Black and working-class women.

Synthesis means showing that these topics are not isolated incidents but together form a pattern that either supports or challenges the overall historical argument. Examiners reward students who can hold the whole unit in their head and deploy evidence selectively to build an argument, rather than students who write everything they know about one topic.
